*Interrogator dossier — capital-allocation committee. Transcripts span FY2025 Q3 (2025-05-07) through FY2026 Q3 (2026-05-06); financials per the screener scan + FMP TTM (2026-03-31).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across six consecutive calls the core story is remarkably **stable in substance but shifts decisively in tone and framing** — from "transformation gathering momentum, still losing share" to "the strategy worked, share has inflected, AI is a tailwind not a threat."

- **FY25 Q3–Q4 (May–Aug 2025) — defensive, "not declaring victory."** Jeff Jones repeatedly conceded the central wound: assisted volume *down 0.8%* against IRS industry growth of ~1.7% (Q3), and in Q4 the FY26 guide's *midpoint assumed share losses merely "cut in half,"* with only the *top* of the range assuming flat share. Beat-and-raise; assisted volume +2.1% / NAC +3.9% ("healthiest balance… in some time"); Second Look returners +600bps retention; product attach +550bps; Sidekick (OpenAI-built tax-pro AI) launched; CNET "best use of AI." - **What management is NOT being pushed on, but should be:** absolute FCF stagnation and the negative/declining book value (buyback-above-book). Analysts treat per-share EPS growth at face value; nobody is interrogating that the *cash engine itself* is flat.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 **Assisted share inflected from −0.8% to flat/+2.1%** (FY26 Q3) — the turnaround thesis delivered on the guided timeline.

🔴 **Negative/hollowed book value** (BVPS 5y CAGR −23.3%; ROE 696.8% is an artifact, not quality). Net debt $1.14B; Altman-Z 2.8 (grey zone). The balance sheet is leveraged to fund returns — fine while FCF holds, fragile if a season ever disappoints.

🔴 **The AI bear case is unfalsified, only deferred** — the turnaround is real, but the terminal question (does gen-AI eventually compress the 55%-seek-assistance constant?) is a multi-year tail the financials cannot yet resolve.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

bull_thesis:
H&R Block is a stable, cash-rich tax-preparation franchise that the market has priced as a business on its way out, and the season just completed is the first hard evidence that it is not. At $41.85 a share (New York Stock Exchange, 2026-07-16 close), the company trades at roughly 8.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 6.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), with a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield and a 13.6% earnings yield. Those multiples belong on a melting asset. The operating record does not match them: revenue grew 5.3% in the March 2026 quarter, earnings per share grew 23% year over year, trailing-twelve-month earnings per share reached $5.60, gross margin held at 44.5%, and returns on invested capital sit between 25% and 39% and are steady rather than falling.

The load-bearing fact is what happened during the 2026 tax season. For three years the bear case had one concrete prediction: that conversational artificial intelligence would hollow out paid tax preparation. The 2026 season was the first full test of that prediction, with capable AI freely available to every filer in America and a major tax-law overhaul reshaping returns. The business grew through it. On the May 2026 call, chief executive Curtis Campbell reported that the company held its share of the assisted (in-person, professional-prepared) channel for the first time after years of losses, and that share performance was favorable in every single week of the season. Assisted volume rose 2.1% and net average charge rose 3.9% - a low-single-digit price increase plus a richer client mix, not price-gouging a shrinking base. Chief financial officer Tiffany Mason called it the healthiest balance of volume, price and mix in years. The company beat on both revenue and earnings and raised its full-year outlook.

The structural argument beneath this is more interesting than the quarter. Campbell separates tax preparation into a mechanical part (collecting documents, entering data, computing) and a relational part (trust, judgment, and accountability for the outcome). AI automates the first. It cannot yet supply the second, because there is no one to hold responsible when a return is wrong. Roughly 55% of American filers have chosen assistance through every prior technology shift - paper to desktop software to online to mobile to early machine learning - and that share has stayed remarkably constant. If Campbell is right, AI is a margin expander here: the Sidekick assistant, built with OpenAI and rolled out this season, removes data-entry work from more than 60,000 tax professionals whose main competitor is the local independent accountant with no AI budget at all. Management is explicit that the real competition is not Intuit but the fragmented independent category - which is precisely the cohort a scaled, AI-equipped operator should take share from.

The recent tax-law overhaul is a demonstrated tailwind rather than a hoped-for one: average client refunds rose about 11%, clients receiving a refund rose about 7%, clients owing money fell more than 25%, and the company enrolled over 2 million of the new 538A accounts, about 90% of eligible clients. Complexity pushes people toward professionals, and management guided this cautiously - using a 20-basis-point channel shift as its proxy - rather than promising it.

Capital allocation is heavy and shareholder-friendly: more than sixty consecutive years of dividends, a 12% raise in August 2025 to $0.42 a quarter, roughly 6% of shares retired in the September 2025 quarter alone, nearly $5B returned since 2016, and an incremental buyback announced May 6, 2026 into the depressed price. Franchise acquisitions - about 150 in fiscal 2026 versus 124 the prior year - quietly convert an 8% royalty into 100% of a location's economics at what management calls attractive multiples.

Coverage has collapsed to almost nothing: zero price targets published in the last quarter, the newest 160 days old. That is why a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield can persist in plain sight. Conditions the case depends on: assisted share must hold again in the 2027 season; net average charge must keep rising on mix rather than on price alone; free cash flow must stop declining once franchise-acquisition spend is bridged; and the board must re-authorize a meaningful buyback in August.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that H&R Block is a bad business. It is that the business is a well-run annuity sitting directly in front of the most capable automation technology ever built, carrying a balance sheet with no shock absorber, and that one good season proves far less than the bulls think.

Start with the cash. Free cash flow fell 8.9% year over year and has compounded at negative 7.1% over three years - while earnings per share compounded at positive 10.9%. That gap is the whole game. Earnings-per-share growth here is substantially manufactured by retiring shares, not by the underlying cash engine expanding. Part of the decline is franchise buybacks, which are a legitimate investment. But management has never bridged it, no analyst has ever asked about it across five consecutive calls, and a company that is buying back stock with a shrinking cash line is drawing down a finite resource. Strip out the buyback and the growth story is a 2.8% three-year revenue compound rate - below the bottom of the 3% to 6% long-term algorithm management keeps reaffirming.

The balance sheet removes the margin for error. Tangible asset value is negative $1.12B. Working capital is negative. Net debt is $1.14B including capitalized leases ($813M excluding them). Altman-Z, a standard solvency score, sits at 2.9, in the grey zone. The much-touted return on equity of 696.8% is not a quality signal at all - it is arithmetic from a book-equity base that buybacks have driven through zero. This structure is optimized for a stable annuity. If the annuity proves unstable, the equity is levered to the downside in a way the 6.1x multiple actively disguises.

On the secular threat, the bull rebuttal proves less than claimed. One season is one data point, and the frog-boiling version of this thesis looks exactly like 2026 in year one: do-it-yourself quietly commoditized first (already visible - online paid volume was essentially flat in the 2025 season, and management chose to walk away from free filers rather than compete), then AI-equipped independents undercut the assisted channel, then the complex, high-income cohort that management has staked the entire strategy on discovers that an AI can handle a complicated return. That sequence takes five years. Campbell's 55% constant is a historical analogy, not a forecast - paper, desktop, and mobile all changed the interface to the calculation, while a large language model can replace the preparer. Management has never once quantified the downside: not a sensitivity, not a scenario, not a number, across five calls. When Sami Nasir asked directly in February 2026 whether the company's own AI tools would cannibalize its assisted business, the entire answer was that they do not think so. A qualitative history lesson is being offered in place of a quantitative risk disclosure, and thin coverage means nobody forces the issue.

The insider record is the loudest signal in the file and it points down. Zero open-market purchases against 13 sells totalling 675,730 shares. Not one officer or director has bought a single share with their own money - during a stretch when the board called the price a dislocation and spent shareholder money on it. When management's core argument is that the market misunderstands the terminal value, the cheapest possible way to prove it is a personal purchase. None has been made.

Capital allocation has also been badly timed on price. The company spent $400M buying stock at an average of $50.90 in the September 2025 quarter. It trades at $41.85 today - roughly $70M transferred to selling shareholders. And the celebrated share stabilization is a floor, not growth: Mason stated plainly in February 2026 that holding share is the high end of the guidance range. Management hit the top of its own range. That is good execution; it is not an inflection to growth, and the stock has already paid for it - up roughly 49% off the $28.16 low and 26% on the May print alone.

What would confirm the bear case: assisted share resuming its decline in the 2027 season, especially in the over-$100,000 income cohort; net average charge growth decelerating toward pure price with mix flattening; free cash flow declining again in fiscal 2027 after franchise spend is accounted for; a weak or absent buyback re-authorization in August signalling the cash is needed elsewhere; or continued insider selling into any strength.
consensus_delta:
The street is not looking the wrong way so much as it has stopped looking at all - and that is the more exploitable condition.

The hard evidence: zero price targets have been published on H&R Block in the last month and zero in the last quarter. The newest is 160 days old. The $41.00 consensus is a stale artifact of two targets set in early February 2026 - Goldman Sachs at $32.00 (2026-02-06, stock then $33.69) and Alexander Paris at $50.00 (2026-02-04, stock then $37.00) - both struck BEFORE the May 6 season results that answered the central question. That consensus mathematically predates the only fact that matters. Anyone citing a $41.00 target as a market view is citing a number formed in ignorance of the 2026 tax season.

Where the market is specifically wrong: the price embeds terminal decline in a business whose earnings power is stable and growing. At $41.85 the stock carries a 13.6% earnings yield and a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield at 6.1x enterprise value to EBITDA. That is distressed pricing. The financials are not distressed: revenue +5.3% in the latest quarter, earnings per share +23% year over year, trailing earnings per share of $5.60, gross margin stable at 44.5%, returns on invested capital of 25-39% and steady, net income at a five-year high, and a raised outlook. The market is paying a melting-ice-cube multiple for a business whose ice is not melting.

The precise assumption that is factually wrong: that the 2026 tax season would show AI taking share. It did not. This was the first full season in which capable conversational AI was freely available to every filer in America, and it coincided with a major tax-law overhaul - maximum disruption conditions. The assisted channel HELD share, and held it favorably in every single week. Volume rose 2.1%. Refunds rose 11%. The bear case had one testable prediction and it failed its first test. Consensus has not marked this to market because there is nobody left publishing.

Where we are careful not to overclaim - and this is what keeps this from being an aggressive entry: the market is not wrong that AI is a genuine structural threat, only that it is an imminent one. One season refutes the cliff, not the slope. And the market has already partly figured this out: the stock is up roughly 49% off its February low and 26% on the May print alone. This is a re-rate in progress, not one waiting to start. The remaining disagreement is worth roughly 31% to our $55 fair value - real, but no longer the 100% gap available in February when the thesis was genuinely contrarian and unpriced.
forcing_function:
The honest answer is that the main forcing function has already fired, and what remains is a dated but ordinary event.

What fired: 2026-05-06. Fiscal third-quarter results delivered the assisted market-share stabilization that was the entire deep-value thesis, plus a double beat and a raised outlook. The stock re-rated about 26% in response. That was the event that was supposed to shatter the terminal-decline consensus, and it did its work.

The next dated event: 2026-08-11, fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year results. Three things land at once - the fiscal-2027 guide, the board's annual dividend review (Mason confirmed in May that the Finance Committee meets over the summer and reports at the August call), and the fiscal-2027 buyback authorization. This is a real date with real content, and it is the specific event to wait for. But it is a scheduled quarterly print with a recurring capital-return review, not a binding corporate action - there is no contractual payout, no deal terms, no proxy contest, no strategic process.

The actual re-rating driver is not a date at all - it is repetition. The bear case dies on evidence, and evidence in this business arrives once a year. The 2027 tax season (filing February-April 2027, reported early May 2027) is when held share becomes a trend rather than a data point. That is the event that converts a 6.1x multiple into a 7.9x multiple, and it is why our horizon is 18 months rather than six.

The speculative options this committee explicitly does NOT credit: a Seeking Alpha piece (2026-07-05) floated divestitures of Wave, Block Advisors and Spruce. That is a writer's suggestion, not a company process - management has announced nothing and reaffirmed its commitment to small business as a growth pillar on every call in the window. Verified today: no activist has surfaced, no strategic review exists, no asset sale is announced. There is a latent activist case (a sum-of-the-parts discount, a loss-making Spruce, a shareholder base that would welcome a sale) but nothing live, and we do not size on hypothetical activism.

The regime tilt cuts against this name and we let it. The current market read ranks the fattest edges in forced-sellers and spinoffs, then activism, and explicitly favors structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes. H&R Block is none of these - it is a compounder at a discount, a shape the current regime deprioritizes. The one genuine regime point in its favor is book independence: in a dispersion tape where an AI-capex guide-down at late-July hyperscaler earnings is the single dominant shared factor that could swamp the book, H&R Block is not merely uncorrelated to it - it is inversely exposed, since AI fear is what created this discount. That is a real diversification argument. It is not a catalyst, and we do not score it as one.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain a specific, identifiable and largely mechanical flush - and it is the reason this is a wait rather than a buy.

First and most important: the company's own bid is gone. On the November 2025 call, Mason said the $400M repurchase in the September quarter completed the share repurchase plan for fiscal 2026, retiring about 6% of shares. An incremental fiscal-2026 authorization was added on 2026-05-06 and will be consumed by the June quarter. Fiscal 2026 ends 2026-06-30. Until the board authorizes a fiscal-2027 program - a decision the Finance Committee makes over the summer and announces with the 2026-08-11 results - the single largest and most price-insensitive buyer of this stock is absent. A company that retired 6% of itself in one quarter withdrawing from its own tape is a material change to the supply-demand balance, and it is not a headline anyone will write.

Second: the seasonal loss window. This is a violently seasonal business. The September quarter (fiscal first quarter 2027, reporting around early November 2026) contributes just over 5% of annual revenue and structurally prints a large loss - fiscal 2026's first quarter showed a $170M EBITDA loss and a $165M net loss on $204M of revenue. So the sequence ahead is: an August print, then three months of no tax-season news, a large seasonal loss print in November, and no buyback support unless re-authorized. Mason even flagged that fiscal-2026 fourth-quarter results carry shifted marketing spend from the third quarter plus peak April field-labor costs - so the August print faces a genuine cost drag against a $2.23 consensus.

Third: the guidance reset risk. Consensus already sits at $5.16 for fiscal 2026 - above the original guided ceiling of $5.00 - and $5.82 for fiscal 2027. That fiscal-2027 number is set by just two analysts. If the initial fiscal-2027 guide on 2026-08-11 lands merely in line, a stock that has run 49% off its low has nothing to reward. The long-term algorithm management keeps reaffirming (3-6% revenue growth) is above the actual three-year record of 2.8%, so an honest guide is arithmetically likely to disappoint the algorithm.

Fourth: the dividend review is genuinely open. Mason declined to pre-commit in May 2026, saying only that the Finance Committee would weigh capital allocation in priority order. A maintained-but-not-raised dividend, after a 12% raise last August, would read as caution to a shareholder base that owns this substantially for yield.

What is NOT a risk here, and should be said: there is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. The business generates $761M of trailing free cash flow, net debt to EBITDA is a comfortable 1.09x, and the seasonal loss is a working-capital rhythm, not distress. The valley of death here is a sentiment and flow event, not a solvency event.
positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling risk here is modest and mostly runs the other way - which argues against expecting a deep flush.

The shareholder base is yield-and-value oriented: more than sixty consecutive years of dividends, a roughly 4% yield, and a stock that screens at the top of every value and shareholder-yield list (Zacks has it at a top rank, and it appeared in June 2026 screens explicitly framed around solid shareholder yield amid AI valuation concerns). That base is sticky and does not liquidate mechanically unless the dividend is cut - and there is no evidence of that. The dividend was RAISED 12% in August 2025, the $0.42 quarterly payment declared 2026-05-04 was paid on 2026-07-07, and it is comfortably covered by $761M of free cash flow. So the classic forced-liquidation trigger for a yield base is absent. This is not a pivot story and there is no dividend cut to force anyone out.

The forced-selling that already happened is the interesting part. The February 2026 flush to $28.16 was the washout - AI fear driving indiscriminate exit from anything a language model might touch, in a tape (per the current regime read) where single names re-rate violently on events and beta is dead. The stock is now 49% off that low. The washout is behind us, not ahead, and that is precisely why this is not an aggressive entry: we are being asked to pay up 49% for evidence that has already been published.

The live flow risk is the reverse of a washout - it is a buyer's absence, not a seller's panic. The company retired about 6% of its shares in one quarter at an average of $50.90 and completed its fiscal-2026 plan; that bid steps away until a fiscal-2027 authorization lands on 2026-08-11. There is also a fast-money overhang from the Zacks rank-one crowd that piled in through June - momentum holders who did not underwrite the structural argument and will leave on an in-line August print.

The positioning signal that deserves the most weight is the insider record, and it is unambiguous: zero open-market buys against 13 sells totalling 675,730 shares. Not a single officer or director has bought a share with their own money - through the February collapse, through the board calling the price a dislocation, through the May vindication. That is not forced selling; it is voluntary, informed, one-directional selling. It does not refute the thesis, but it means the people with the best view of the AI question have chosen cash over conviction at these levels, and no position here should be sized as though management is alongside us.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good business at a genuinely cheap price whose catalyst already fired, and the discipline this committee owes the capital is to say both halves of that sentence.

The value is real. At $41.85 (New York Stock Exchange, 2026-07-16 close) H&R Block trades at 8.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 6.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA, with a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield, a 13.6% earnings yield, returns on invested capital between 25% and 39%, stable 44.5% gross margins, a Piotroski score of 7 out of 9, and more than sixty consecutive years of dividends. Our sum-of-the-parts work puts fair value at $55 - about 31% above the current price - with an adverse case of $31 and a favorable case of $70. The evidence supports the business, not the price. Management beat and raised. Chief executive Curtis Campbell, four months into the job, delivered the one thing his predecessor could not. The moat is narrow but real - brand, ~9,000 offices, 60,000 professionals, and an accountability guarantee AI cannot yet offer - and the returns evidence forbids calling it eroding, because eroding moats show falling returns and compressing margins while this one shows neither. On that basis, and with the secular threat material rather than terminal, the value case earns a 4: this is a fear-print, not a value trap.

But the catalyst is spent, and that is what caps the execution call. The May 6 print WAS the re-rate. The stock is up roughly 49% off its February low and 26% on that single day. We are being asked to pay up for evidence that is already public. The remaining event - the August 11 results with the fiscal-2027 guide, the annual dividend review and the buyback authorization - is a dated but ordinary quarterly print, not a binding catalyst. And the current regime read explicitly ranks forced-sellers, spinoffs and activism as the fattest lanes while deprioritizing exactly this shape: a compounder at a discount with no corporate action behind it. We let the regime move the number down rather than arguing with it.

Three things keep the conviction at 3 rather than 4. Free cash flow is declining 8.9% year over year and negative 7.1% compounded over three years while earnings per share compounds at positive 10.9% - substantially franchise-acquisition spend, but unbridged by management and unasked-about by analysts across five straight calls. When the whole argument is that the market misprices your terminal value, a personal purchase is the cheapest possible proof, and none has been made.

So: wait for the wash-out, and the wash-out has a name and a mechanism. The company completed its fiscal-2026 buyback plan - the bid that retired 6% of the shares in a single quarter steps away until the board re-authorizes on August 11. Then comes a seasonally brutal September quarter (fiscal 2026 first quarter printed a $170M EBITDA loss on $204M of revenue), reported around early November, with no tax-season news in between and a momentum crowd from June's screens that did not underwrite the structural argument. That September-to-November window - no corporate bid, a large seasonal loss, no news - is where this gets bought.

Our estimate of fair value is $55 on an 18-month horizon, because the bear case dies on evidence and evidence in this business arrives once a year: the 2027 season, reported May 2027, is when held share becomes a trend rather than a data point. Note there is no floor beneath the $31 downside - no deal terms, no net cash, no breakup value, and the 4% yield is not a floor and is not treated as one. Size for the possibility that Campbell's structural argument is wrong, not for the probability that it is right. One season is one data point, and the slow version of the AI thesis looks exactly like 2026 in year one.

The peer file offers one comparable, Intuit, and correctly refuses to lean on it. Intuit trades above 30x free cash flow against H&R Block's 8.5x, but it is a diversified software platform (TurboTax plus QuickBooks, Credit Karma and Mailchimp), not a tax-preparation peer. The true direct competitors - Jackson Hewitt and Liberty Tax - are privately held and print no multiple. The peer verdict of cheap-versus-peers is therefore built on H&R Block's own high-return, positive-margin-of-safety profile rather than on a tight comparable multiple, and the file says so plainly. No peer_override or anchor_multiple was supplied.

This matters for how much credit the discount earns. A 22-point multiple gap to Intuit is not evidence of anything - it is a category error, and management said so themselves on the May 2025 call: the number one competitor in assisted tax is the independent accountant category, by far, not Intuit. Our valuation therefore anchors on H&R Block's own history (roughly 9-11x enterprise value to EBITDA before the AI de-rating, versus 6.1x today) and on its absolute cash economics - a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield and 25-39% returns on invested capital - rather than on the peer gap. The multiple we underwrite (7.95x blended in the base case) is deliberately below the company's own historical range, not at Intuit's.

bull_thesis:
H&R Block is a stable, cash-rich tax-preparation franchise that the market has priced as a business on its way out, and the season just completed is the first hard evidence that it is not. At $41.85 a share (New York Stock Exchange, 2026-07-16 close), the company trades at roughly 8.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 6.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), with a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield and a 13.6% earnings yield. Those multiples belong on a melting asset. The operating record does not match them: revenue grew 5.3% in the March 2026 quarter, earnings per share grew 23% year over year, trailing-twelve-month earnings per share reached $5.60, gross margin held at 44.5%, and returns on invested capital sit between 25% and 39% and are steady rather than falling.

The load-bearing fact is what happened during the 2026 tax season. For three years the bear case had one concrete prediction: that conversational artificial intelligence would hollow out paid tax preparation. The 2026 season was the first full test of that prediction, with capable AI freely available to every filer in America and a major tax-law overhaul reshaping returns. The business grew through it. On the May 2026 call, chief executive Curtis Campbell reported that the company held its share of the assisted (in-person, professional-prepared) channel for the first time after years of losses, and that share performance was favorable in every single week of the season. Assisted volume rose 2.1% and net average charge rose 3.9% - a low-single-digit price increase plus a richer client mix, not price-gouging a shrinking base. Chief financial officer Tiffany Mason called it the healthiest balance of volume, price and mix in years. The company beat on both revenue and earnings and raised its full-year outlook.

The structural argument beneath this is more interesting than the quarter. Campbell separates tax preparation into a mechanical part (collecting documents, entering data, computing) and a relational part (trust, judgment, and accountability for the outcome). AI automates the first. It cannot yet supply the second, because there is no one to hold responsible when a return is wrong. Roughly 55% of American filers have chosen assistance through every prior technology shift - paper to desktop software to online to mobile to early machine learning - and that share has stayed remarkably constant. If Campbell is right, AI is a margin expander here: the Sidekick assistant, built with OpenAI and rolled out this season, removes data-entry work from more than 60,000 tax professionals whose main competitor is the local independent accountant with no AI budget at all. Management is explicit that the real competition is not Intuit but the fragmented independent category - which is precisely the cohort a scaled, AI-equipped operator should take share from.

The recent tax-law overhaul is a demonstrated tailwind rather than a hoped-for one: average client refunds rose about 11%, clients receiving a refund rose about 7%, clients owing money fell more than 25%, and the company enrolled over 2 million of the new 538A accounts, about 90% of eligible clients. Complexity pushes people toward professionals, and management guided this cautiously - using a 20-basis-point channel shift as its proxy - rather than promising it.

Capital allocation is heavy and shareholder-friendly: more than sixty consecutive years of dividends, a 12% raise in August 2025 to $0.42 a quarter, roughly 6% of shares retired in the September 2025 quarter alone, nearly $5B returned since 2016, and an incremental buyback announced May 6, 2026 into the depressed price. Franchise acquisitions - about 150 in fiscal 2026 versus 124 the prior year - quietly convert an 8% royalty into 100% of a location's economics at what management calls attractive multiples.

Coverage has collapsed to almost nothing: zero price targets published in the last quarter, the newest 160 days old. That is why a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield can persist in plain sight. Conditions the case depends on: assisted share must hold again in the 2027 season; net average charge must keep rising on mix rather than on price alone; free cash flow must stop declining once franchise-acquisition spend is bridged; and the board must re-authorize a meaningful buyback in August.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that H&R Block is a bad business. It is that the business is a well-run annuity sitting directly in front of the most capable automation technology ever built, carrying a balance sheet with no shock absorber, and that one good season proves far less than the bulls think.

Start with the cash. Free cash flow fell 8.9% year over year and has compounded at negative 7.1% over three years - while earnings per share compounded at positive 10.9%. That gap is the whole game. Earnings-per-share growth here is substantially manufactured by retiring shares, not by the underlying cash engine expanding. Part of the decline is franchise buybacks, which are a legitimate investment. But management has never bridged it, no analyst has ever asked about it across five consecutive calls, and a company that is buying back stock with a shrinking cash line is drawing down a finite resource. Strip out the buyback and the growth story is a 2.8% three-year revenue compound rate - below the bottom of the 3% to 6% long-term algorithm management keeps reaffirming.

The balance sheet removes the margin for error. Tangible asset value is negative $1.12B. Working capital is negative. Net debt is $1.14B including capitalized leases ($813M excluding them). Altman-Z, a standard solvency score, sits at 2.9, in the grey zone. The much-touted return on equity of 696.8% is not a quality signal at all - it is arithmetic from a book-equity base that buybacks have driven through zero. This structure is optimized for a stable annuity. If the annuity proves unstable, the equity is levered to the downside in a way the 6.1x multiple actively disguises.

On the secular threat, the bull rebuttal proves less than claimed. One season is one data point, and the frog-boiling version of this thesis looks exactly like 2026 in year one: do-it-yourself quietly commoditized first (already visible - online paid volume was essentially flat in the 2025 season, and management chose to walk away from free filers rather than compete), then AI-equipped independents undercut the assisted channel, then the complex, high-income cohort that management has staked the entire strategy on discovers that an AI can handle a complicated return. That sequence takes five years. Campbell's 55% constant is a historical analogy, not a forecast - paper, desktop, and mobile all changed the interface to the calculation, while a large language model can replace the preparer. Management has never once quantified the downside: not a sensitivity, not a scenario, not a number, across five calls. When Sami Nasir asked directly in February 2026 whether the company's own AI tools would cannibalize its assisted business, the entire answer was that they do not think so. A qualitative history lesson is being offered in place of a quantitative risk disclosure, and thin coverage means nobody forces the issue.

The insider record is the loudest signal in the file and it points down. Zero open-market purchases against 13 sells totalling 675,730 shares. Not one officer or director has bought a single share with their own money - during a stretch when the board called the price a dislocation and spent shareholder money on it. When management's core argument is that the market misunderstands the terminal value, the cheapest possible way to prove it is a personal purchase. None has been made.

Capital allocation has also been badly timed on price. The company spent $400M buying stock at an average of $50.90 in the September 2025 quarter. It trades at $41.85 today - roughly $70M transferred to selling shareholders. And the celebrated share stabilization is a floor, not growth: Mason stated plainly in February 2026 that holding share is the high end of the guidance range. Management hit the top of its own range. That is good execution; it is not an inflection to growth, and the stock has already paid for it - up roughly 49% off the $28.16 low and 26% on the May print alone.

What would confirm the bear case: assisted share resuming its decline in the 2027 season, especially in the over-$100,000 income cohort; net average charge growth decelerating toward pure price with mix flattening; free cash flow declining again in fiscal 2027 after franchise spend is accounted for; a weak or absent buyback re-authorization in August signalling the cash is needed elsewhere; or continued insider selling into any strength.
consensus_delta:
The street is not looking the wrong way so much as it has stopped looking at all - and that is the more exploitable condition.

The hard evidence: zero price targets have been published on H&R Block in the last month and zero in the last quarter. The newest is 160 days old. The $41.00 consensus is a stale artifact of two targets set in early February 2026 - Goldman Sachs at $32.00 (2026-02-06, stock then $33.69) and Alexander Paris at $50.00 (2026-02-04, stock then $37.00) - both struck BEFORE the May 6 season results that answered the central question. That consensus mathematically predates the only fact that matters. Anyone citing a $41.00 target as a market view is citing a number formed in ignorance of the 2026 tax season.

Where the market is specifically wrong: the price embeds terminal decline in a business whose earnings power is stable and growing. At $41.85 the stock carries a 13.6% earnings yield and a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield at 6.1x enterprise value to EBITDA. That is distressed pricing. The financials are not distressed: revenue +5.3% in the latest quarter, earnings per share +23% year over year, trailing earnings per share of $5.60, gross margin stable at 44.5%, returns on invested capital of 25-39% and steady, net income at a five-year high, and a raised outlook. The market is paying a melting-ice-cube multiple for a business whose ice is not melting.

The precise assumption that is factually wrong: that the 2026 tax season would show AI taking share. It did not. The assisted channel HELD share, and held it favorably in every single week. Volume rose 2.1%. Refunds rose 11%. The bear case had one testable prediction and it failed its first test. Consensus has not marked this to market because there is nobody left publishing.

Where we are careful not to overclaim - and this is what keeps this from being an aggressive entry: the market is not wrong that AI is a genuine structural threat, only that it is an imminent one. One season refutes the cliff, not the slope. And the market has already partly figured this out: the stock is up roughly 49% off its February low and 26% on the May print alone. This is a re-rate in progress, not one waiting to start. The remaining disagreement is worth roughly 31% to our $55 fair value - real, but no longer the 100% gap available in February when the thesis was genuinely contrarian and unpriced.
forcing_function:
The honest answer is that the main forcing function has already fired, and what remains is a dated but ordinary event.

What fired: 2026-05-06. Fiscal third-quarter results delivered the assisted market-share stabilization that was the entire deep-value thesis, plus a double beat and a raised outlook. The stock re-rated about 26% in response. That was the event that was supposed to shatter the terminal-decline consensus, and it did its work.

The next dated event: 2026-08-11, fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year results. Three things land at once - the fiscal-2027 guide, the board's annual dividend review (Mason confirmed in May that the Finance Committee meets over the summer and reports at the August call), and the fiscal-2027 buyback authorization. This is a real date with real content, and it is the specific event to wait for. But it is a scheduled quarterly print with a recurring capital-return review, not a binding corporate action - there is no contractual payout, no deal terms, no proxy contest, no strategic process.

The actual re-rating driver is not a date at all - it is repetition. The bear case dies on evidence, and evidence in this business arrives once a year. The 2027 tax season (filing February-April 2027, reported early May 2027) is when held share becomes a trend rather than a data point. That is the event that converts a 6.1x multiple into a 7.9x multiple, and it is why our horizon is 18 months rather than six.

The speculative options this committee explicitly does NOT credit: a Seeking Alpha piece (2026-07-05) floated divestitures of Wave, Block Advisors and Spruce. That is a writer's suggestion, not a company process - management has announced nothing and reaffirmed its commitment to small business as a growth pillar on every call in the window. Verified today: no activist has surfaced, no strategic review exists, no asset sale is announced. There is a latent activist case (a sum-of-the-parts discount, a loss-making Spruce, a shareholder base that would welcome a sale) but nothing live, and we do not size on hypothetical activism.

The regime tilt cuts against this name and we let it. The current market read ranks the fattest edges in forced-sellers and spinoffs, then activism, and explicitly favors structural special situations in thin-coverage lanes. H&R Block is none of these - it is a compounder at a discount, a shape the current regime deprioritizes. The one genuine regime point in its favor is book independence: in a dispersion tape where an AI-capex guide-down at late-July hyperscaler earnings is the single dominant shared factor that could swamp the book, H&R Block is not merely uncorrelated to it - it is inversely exposed, since AI fear is what created this discount. That is a real diversification argument. It is not a catalyst, and we do not score it as one.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain a specific, identifiable and largely mechanical flush - and it is the reason this is a wait rather than a buy.

First and most important: the company's own bid is gone. On the November 2025 call, Mason said the $400M repurchase in the September quarter completed the share repurchase plan for fiscal 2026, retiring about 6% of shares. An incremental fiscal-2026 authorization was added on 2026-05-06 and will be consumed by the June quarter. Fiscal 2026 ends 2026-06-30. Until the board authorizes a fiscal-2027 program - a decision the Finance Committee makes over the summer and announces with the 2026-08-11 results - the single largest and most price-insensitive buyer of this stock is absent. A company that retired 6% of itself in one quarter withdrawing from its own tape is a material change to the supply-demand balance, and it is not a headline anyone will write.

Second: the seasonal loss window. This is a violently seasonal business. The September quarter (fiscal first quarter 2027, reporting around early November 2026) contributes just over 5% of annual revenue and structurally prints a large loss - fiscal 2026's first quarter showed a $170M EBITDA loss and a $165M net loss on $204M of revenue. So the sequence ahead is: an August print, then three months of no tax-season news, a large seasonal loss print in November, and no buyback support unless re-authorized. Mason even flagged that fiscal-2026 fourth-quarter results carry shifted marketing spend from the third quarter plus peak April field-labor costs - so the August print faces a genuine cost drag against a $2.23 consensus.

Third: the guidance reset risk. Consensus already sits at $5.16 for fiscal 2026 - above the original guided ceiling of $5.00 - and $5.82 for fiscal 2027. That fiscal-2027 number is set by just two analysts. If the initial fiscal-2027 guide on 2026-08-11 lands merely in line, a stock that has run 49% off its low has nothing to reward. The long-term algorithm management keeps reaffirming (3-6% revenue growth) is above the actual three-year record of 2.8%, so an honest guide is arithmetically likely to disappoint the algorithm.

Fourth: the dividend review is genuinely open. Mason declined to pre-commit in May 2026, saying only that the Finance Committee would weigh capital allocation in priority order. A maintained-but-not-raised dividend, after a 12% raise last August, would read as caution to a shareholder base that owns this substantially for yield.

What is NOT a risk here, and should be said: there is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall. The business generates $761M of trailing free cash flow, net debt to EBITDA is a comfortable 1.09x, and the seasonal loss is a working-capital rhythm, not distress. The valley of death here is a sentiment and flow event, not a solvency event.
positioning_washout:
The mechanical selling risk here is modest and mostly runs the other way - which argues against expecting a deep flush.

The shareholder base is yield-and-value oriented: more than sixty consecutive years of dividends, a roughly 4% yield, and a stock that screens at the top of every value and shareholder-yield list (Zacks has it at a top rank, and it appeared in June 2026 screens explicitly framed around solid shareholder yield amid AI valuation concerns). That base is sticky and does not liquidate mechanically unless the dividend is cut - and there is no evidence of that. The dividend was RAISED 12% in August 2025, the $0.42 quarterly payment declared 2026-05-04 was paid on 2026-07-07, and it is comfortably covered by $761M of free cash flow. So the classic forced-liquidation trigger for a yield base is absent. This is not a pivot story and there is no dividend cut to force anyone out.

The forced-selling that already happened is the interesting part. The February 2026 flush to $28.16 was the washout - AI fear driving indiscriminate exit from anything a language model might touch, in a tape (per the current regime read) where single names re-rate violently on events and beta is dead. The stock is now 49% off that low. The washout is behind us, not ahead, and that is precisely why this is not an aggressive entry: we are being asked to pay up 49% for evidence that has already been published.

The live flow risk is the reverse of a washout - it is a buyer's absence, not a seller's panic. The company retired about 6% of its shares in one quarter at an average of $50.90 and completed its fiscal-2026 plan; that bid steps away until a fiscal-2027 authorization lands on 2026-08-11. There is also a fast-money overhang from the Zacks rank-one crowd that piled in through June - momentum holders who did not underwrite the structural argument and will leave on an in-line August print.

The positioning signal that deserves the most weight is the insider record, and it is unambiguous: zero open-market buys against 13 sells totalling 675,730 shares. Not a single officer or director has bought a share with their own money - through the February collapse, through the board calling the price a dislocation, through the May vindication. That is not forced selling; it is voluntary, informed, one-directional selling. It does not refute the thesis, but it means the people with the best view of the AI question have chosen cash over conviction at these levels, and no position here should be sized as though management is alongside us.

This is a good business at a genuinely cheap price whose catalyst already fired, and the discipline this committee owes the capital is to say both halves of that sentence.

interrogator_dossier:
# H&R Block (HRB) — Forensic Dossier

*Six consecutive earnings calls, May 2025 (fiscal Q3 2025) through May 2026 (fiscal Q3 2026), cross-referenced against the screener financials. H&R Block runs an April 30 fiscal year, so "fiscal 2026" is the tax season that just closed. Live price used: about $40.58 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars).*

## 1. Narrative Arc

The story management tells has been remarkably steady across these six quarters, which is itself the point: this is a slow, stable franchise, not a turnaround with a moving thesis. The through-line is "expert-led, technology-enabled" tax preparation — the idea that most Americans will keep paying a human for confidence and accountability even as software gets better, and that H&R Block's job is to use artificial intelligence to make its tax professionals faster rather than to replace them.

What did shift over the year is emphasis. In the first two calls (May and August 2025), the dominant theme was *defending assisted market share* — management repeatedly conceded it was "not ready to declare victory yet" on share, having improved conversion and retention for two straight years but still losing ground to the independent tax preparers. By the November 2025 and February 2026 calls, incoming chief executive Curtis Campbell (who took over from Jeff Jones on January 1, 2026) reframed the business around a "multiyear journey" to strip manual work out of the tax professional's day using AI, with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (a 2025 tax-law overhaul) positioned as a complexity tailwind that pushes do-it-yourself filers toward assisted help. By the May 2026 call, the arc reached its payoff: management declared that assisted market share *stabilized* in the 2026 season — "this season, we did" — after two years of narrowing losses. ## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Trajectory: Rising, then confirmed.** The tone climbed steadily from cautious ("we still have work to do," May 2025) to vindicated ("strong results ahead of expectations across all key metrics… we are raising our full year outlook," May 2026). **Reliability: High.** The screener records a 71% earnings-beat rate (5 of 7 quarters). The recurring pressure point all year was **assisted market-share loss** — George Tong of Goldman Sachs pressed on it call after call (assisted volume down 0.8% versus ~1.7% industry growth in May 2025). Management's answer was always "improving trajectory, not yet victory," which finally paid off in May 2026. Management's rebuttal is consistent and evidence-based: ~55% of ~150M US filers have sought assistance for decades, a share "fairly constant through paper to desktop to online to mobile to machine learning to Gen 1 AI," because people want confidence and accountability, not arithmetic. That is a genuinely strong answer, but it is a *thesis about the future*, and it is the exact fault line on which the stock is priced. Notably, no topic analysts pushed on later turned into bad news this year — the reverse of the usual red-flag pattern.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 Free cash flow is *declining* (~-9% year-over-year, ~-7% a year over three years) even as earnings per share rise — the gap between reported earnings growth and cash generation deserves scrutiny.
🔴 Insiders are net sellers: zero open-market buys against 13 sells (~676k shares). No management conviction is showing up in personal buying.
🔴 Organic volume growth is essentially nil — the franchise grows revenue ~4% on price/mix and shrinks the share count; it does not grow filers.

🟢 Beat-and-raise in May 2026; 5-of-7 beat rate; transparent, specific guidance.
🟢 Second Look lifted new-client retention by 600+ basis points — a real, measured loyalty mechanism.
🟢 Aggressive, opportunistic buybacks *into* the AI-fear price dislocation (management bought ~6% of the company in one quarter near $51; the stock later traded as low as ~$28).
🟢 Smooth, pre-planned internal chief-executive succession — strategy explicitly "locked," no discontinuity risk.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The subtlest shift is linguistic: under new chief executive Campbell, "expert-led, technology-enabled" hardened from a slogan into a two-component framework — the "mechanical" work (data entry, calculation) that AI will commoditize, versus the "relational" work (trust, judgment, accountability) that AI cannot. This is management pre-positioning the moat where it is most defensible and conceding the ground where it is not — an honest, sophisticated framing rather than blanket denial. A second signal: the deliberate, repeated distinction between "free forever" DIY filers (low lifetime value, ceded to competitors) and paying/convertible clients (the only ones they will spend to win) — a disciplined refusal to chase vanity market-share metrics, even at the cost of headline volume. On capital allocation the pecking order was restated verbatim every quarter: invest in the business, then grow the dividend, then buy back stock — no drift.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a mature, high-return, cash-generative franchise executing well and returning capital aggressively — not a company that is strengthening dramatically or deteriorating. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the entire valuation debate is a bet on one thesis — that artificial intelligence does not structurally erode the assisted tax-prep base over the next five to ten years.** The 2026 share stabilization is real, dated evidence for that thesis; the declining free cash flow and nil organic volume growth are the evidence against. Everything else (the buybacks, the dividend, the ~8x earnings multiple) is second-order to that one question.

**Moat:** intangible-brand plus switching-cost — a 70-year trusted brand, ~9,000 offices within five miles of most Americans, ~60,000 tax pros averaging ten years' tenure, and returning-client stickiness reinforced by Second Look. Judged on the evidence, this is a **narrow but real** moat: the 25% return on invested capital and stable ~44.5% gross margin say the economics are intact and not visibly eroding *yet*, but flat organic profit and years of share loss (only just arrested) say it is not widening either. **Moat trend: stable.** **Secular threat: material** — AI-driven do-it-yourself displacement is a genuine, multi-year overhang on the terminal value (it is why the stock trades at a single-digit multiple), but management's evidence that assistance-seeking has held constant through every prior technology wave, plus the 2026 share stabilization, argues it is a fear-print worth a discount rather than a confirmed melting base. interrogator_dossier:
# H&R Block (HRB) — Forensic Dossier

*Six consecutive earnings calls, May 2025 (fiscal Q3 2025) through May 2026 (fiscal Q3 2026), cross-referenced against the screener financials. H&R Block runs an April 30 fiscal year, so "fiscal 2026" is the tax season that just closed. Live price used: about $40.58 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars).*

## 1. Narrative Arc

The story management tells has been remarkably steady across these six quarters, which is itself the point: this is a slow, stable franchise, not a turnaround with a moving thesis. The through-line is "expert-led, technology-enabled" tax preparation — the idea that most Americans will keep paying a human for confidence and accountability even as software gets better, and that H&R Block's job is to use artificial intelligence to make its tax professionals faster rather than to replace them.

What did shift over the year is emphasis. In the first two calls (May and August 2025), the dominant theme was *defending assisted market share* — management repeatedly conceded it was "not ready to declare victory yet" on share, having improved conversion and retention for two straight years but still losing ground to the independent tax preparers. By the November 2025 and February 2026 calls, incoming chief executive Curtis Campbell (who took over from Jeff Jones on January 1, 2026) reframed the business around a "multiyear journey" to strip manual work out of the tax professional's day using AI, with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (a 2025 tax-law overhaul) positioned as a complexity tailwind that pushes do-it-yourself filers toward assisted help. By the May 2026 call, the arc reached its payoff: management declared that assisted market share *stabilized* in the 2026 season — "this season, we did" — after two years of narrowing losses. That is the single most important narrative event of the year.

Growth levers introduced or amplified: Second Look (a free review of a new client's prior three years of returns), scaled this year from a niche manual offering into a core, AI-automated onboarding step that lifted new-client retention by more than 600 basis points; Sidekick, an AI assistant for tax pros built with OpenAI; and Wave (small-business software) growing double digits. Nothing material was quietly dropped — the consistency is a credibility marker.

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Consistent growth" / healthy franchise | Revenue $3.46B → $3.76B over 2021–2025 (~+2% a year), +4.2% in fiscal 2025 | Matches, but "growth" is generous — this is a low-single-digit top line |
| Double-digit earnings growth | Earnings per share $2.94 → $4.39 (2021–2025); trailing-twelve-month diluted $5.60 | True, but see below — it is engineered |
| Strong cash generation | Trailing free cash flow $761M; but free cash flow fell about 9% year-over-year and roughly 7% a year over three years | Mixed — cash is real but the trend is *down*, a genuine yellow flag |
| Disciplined capital return | Retired ~6% of shares in fiscal-Q1 2026 alone (~$400M at ~$50.90); dividend raised to $0.42/quarter (~4% yield); ~$5B returned since 2016 | Fully corroborated — this is the strongest, most verifiable claim |
| Share stabilized in 2026 | Assisted volume +2.1%, net average charge +3.9% in the season | Corroborated by the operating stats management disclosed |

The forensic tension: net income was essentially *flat* from 2021 to 2023 ($554M each year) before rising to $606M in 2025. Almost all of the double-digit earnings-per-share growth comes from shrinking the share count, not from growing the profit pool. That is a legitimate, shareholder-friendly strategy for a mature cash cow — but it means the "growth" narrative is richer than the underlying earnings trajectory justifies. Book value per share has gone *negative* and fallen ~23% a year, the arithmetic signature of a company buying back so much stock that equity is negative; the eye-popping 696.8% return on equity is that same artifact, not a sign of exceptional economics (the cleaner figure is the 25.1% return on invested capital, which is genuinely strong). Net debt is about $1.14B including leases (~$0.81B excluding them) — a liability, not a war chest.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Trajectory: Rising, then confirmed.** The tone climbed steadily from cautious ("we still have work to do," May 2025) to vindicated ("strong results ahead of expectations across all key metrics… we are raising our full year outlook," May 2026). The most telling shift is on market share: for four calls management hedged with "not ready to declare victory"; in May 2026 it stated flatly that share held and "was favorable each week throughout the entire season." Guidance became *more* specific over the year, not less — a confidence signal. Language stayed offensive (growth, investment, AI opportunity) rather than defensive (cost-cutting, macro excuses), with the one exception of honest discussion of elevated fiscal-2025 legal, healthcare and severance costs, which management then bridged transparently into the fiscal-2026 guide.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Reliability: High.** The screener records a 71% earnings-beat rate (5 of 7 quarters). Management reaffirmed its fiscal-2026 outlook at the August and November 2025 calls, then *raised* it in May 2026 after the tax season came in ahead of plan — a beat-and-raise, the most credible pattern there is. The chief financial officer, Tiffany Mason, walked analysts through the fiscal-2025 cost overruns (healthcare, legal, severance) and showed exactly how each was normalized in the fiscal-2026 guide; the season then delivered on those assumptions ("industry growth rate is coming in right where we expected"). There is mild sandbagging in the long-term algorithm (3–6% revenue, earnings before interest/taxes/depreciation/amortization at 1.5x that, double-digit earnings-per-share) — they consistently guide conservative and clear the bar.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

The recurring pressure point all year was **assisted market-share loss** — George Tong of Goldman Sachs pressed on it call after call (assisted volume down 0.8% versus ~1.7% industry growth in May 2025). Management's answer was always "improving trajectory, not yet victory," which finally paid off in May 2026. The second recurring worry is the **existential AI/do-it-yourself threat** — analysts asked repeatedly whether easier AI-powered DIY tools cannibalize the assisted business. Management's rebuttal is consistent and evidence-based: ~55% of ~150M US filers have sought assistance for decades, a share "fairly constant through paper to desktop to online to mobile to machine learning to Gen 1 AI," because people want confidence and accountability, not arithmetic. That is a genuinely strong answer, but it is a *thesis about the future*, and it is the exact fault line on which the stock is priced. Notably, no topic analysts pushed on later turned into bad news this year — the reverse of the usual red-flag pattern.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 Free cash flow is *declining* (~-9% year-over-year, ~-7% a year over three years) even as earnings per share rise — the gap between reported earnings growth and cash generation deserves scrutiny.
🔴 Insiders are net sellers: zero open-market buys against 13 sells (~676k shares). No management conviction is showing up in personal buying.
🔴 Organic volume growth is essentially nil — the franchise grows revenue ~4% on price/mix and shrinks the share count; it does not grow filers.
🔴 Negative book equity and ~$1.14B net debt leave no balance-sheet cushion and cap how long the buyback engine can run without leaning on leverage.

🟢 Assisted market share *stabilized* in the 2026 season after two years of losses — the first hard proof-point against the terminal-decline thesis (May 2026).
🟢 Beat-and-raise in May 2026; 5-of-7 beat rate; transparent, specific guidance.
🟢 Second Look lifted new-client retention by 600+ basis points — a real, measured loyalty mechanism.
🟢 Aggressive, opportunistic buybacks *into* the AI-fear price dislocation (management bought ~6% of the company in one quarter near $51; the stock later traded as low as ~$28).
🟢 Smooth, pre-planned internal chief-executive succession — strategy explicitly "locked," no discontinuity risk.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The subtlest shift is linguistic: under new chief executive Campbell, "expert-led, technology-enabled" hardened from a slogan into a two-component framework — the "mechanical" work (data entry, calculation) that AI will commoditize, versus the "relational" work (trust, judgment, accountability) that AI cannot. This is management pre-positioning the moat where it is most defensible and conceding the ground where it is not — an honest, sophisticated framing rather than blanket denial. A second signal: the deliberate, repeated distinction between "free forever" DIY filers (low lifetime value, ceded to competitors) and paying/convertible clients (the only ones they will spend to win) — a disciplined refusal to chase vanity market-share metrics, even at the cost of headline volume. On capital allocation the pecking order was restated verbatim every quarter: invest in the business, then grow the dividend, then buy back stock — no drift.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** This is a mature, high-return, cash-generative franchise executing well and returning capital aggressively — not a company that is strengthening dramatically or deteriorating. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the entire valuation debate is a bet on one thesis — that artificial intelligence does not structurally erode the assisted tax-prep base over the next five to ten years.** The 2026 share stabilization is real, dated evidence for that thesis; the declining free cash flow and nil organic volume growth are the evidence against. Everything else (the buybacks, the dividend, the ~8x earnings multiple) is second-order to that one question.

**Moat:** intangible-brand plus switching-cost — a 70-year trusted brand, ~9,000 offices within five miles of most Americans, ~60,000 tax pros averaging ten years' tenure, and returning-client stickiness reinforced by Second Look. Judged on the evidence, this is a **narrow but real** moat: the 25% return on invested capital and stable ~44.5% gross margin say the economics are intact and not visibly eroding *yet*, but flat organic profit and years of share loss (only just arrested) say it is not widening either. **Moat trend: stable.** **Secular threat: material** — AI-driven do-it-yourself displacement is a genuine, multi-year overhang on the terminal value (it is why the stock trades at a single-digit multiple), but management's evidence that assistance-seeking has held constant through every prior technology wave, plus the 2026 share stabilization, argues it is a fear-print worth a discount rather than a confirmed melting base. The cheapness is therefore *partly* mispricing and *partly* a rational discount for real terminal-value uncertainty — not a clean fat pitch.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: material

bull_thesis:
H&R Block is a stable, cash-rich tax-preparation franchise that the market has priced as a business on its way out, and the season just completed is the first hard evidence that it is not. At $41.85 a share (New York Stock Exchange, 2026-07-16 close), the company trades at roughly 8.5 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 6.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), with a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield and a 13.6% earnings yield. Those multiples belong on a melting asset. The operating record does not match them: revenue grew 5.3% in the March 2026 quarter, earnings per share grew 23% year over year, trailing-twelve-month earnings per share reached $5.60, gross margin held at 44.5%, and returns on invested capital sit between 25% and 39% and are steady rather than falling.

The load-bearing fact is what happened during the 2026 tax season. For three years the bear case had one concrete prediction: that conversational artificial intelligence would hollow out paid tax preparation. The 2026 season was the first full test of that prediction, with capable AI freely available to every filer in America and a major tax-law overhaul reshaping returns. The business grew through it. On the May 2026 call, chief executive Curtis Campbell reported that the company held its share of the assisted (in-person, professional-prepared) channel for the first time after years of losses, and that share performance was favorable in every single week of the season. Assisted volume rose 2.1% and net average charge rose 3.9% - a low-single-digit price increase plus a richer client mix, not price-gouging a shrinking base. Chief financial officer Tiffany Mason called it the healthiest balance of volume, price and mix in years. The company beat on both revenue and earnings and raised its full-year outlook.

The structural argument beneath this is more interesting than the quarter. Campbell separates tax preparation into a mechanical part (collecting documents, entering data, computing) and a relational part (trust, judgment, and accountability for the outcome). AI automates the first. It cannot yet supply the second, because there is no one to hold responsible when a return is wrong. Roughly 55% of American filers have chosen assistance through every prior technology shift - paper to desktop software to online to mobile to early machine learning - and that share has stayed remarkably constant. If Campbell is right, AI is a margin expander here: the Sidekick assistant, built with OpenAI and rolled out this season, removes data-entry work from more than 60,000 tax professionals whose main competitor is the local independent accountant with no AI budget at all. Management is explicit that the real competition is not Intuit but the fragmented independent category - which is precisely the cohort a scaled, AI-equipped operator should take share from.

The recent tax-law overhaul is a demonstrated tailwind rather than a hoped-for one: average client refunds rose about 11%, clients receiving a refund rose about 7%, clients owing money fell more than 25%, and the company enrolled over 2 million of the new 538A accounts, about 90% of eligible clients. Complexity pushes people toward professionals, and management guided this cautiously - using a 20-basis-point channel shift as its proxy - rather than promising it.

Capital allocation is heavy and shareholder-friendly: more than sixty consecutive years of dividends, a 12% raise in August 2025 to $0.42 a quarter, roughly 6% of shares retired in the September 2025 quarter alone, nearly $5B returned since 2016, and an incremental buyback announced May 6, 2026 into the depressed price. Franchise acquisitions - about 150 in fiscal 2026 versus 124 the prior year - quietly convert an 8% royalty into 100% of a location's economics at what management calls attractive multiples.

Coverage has collapsed to almost nothing: zero price targets published in the last quarter, the newest 160 days old. That is why a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield can persist in plain sight. Conditions the case depends on: assisted share must hold again in the 2027 season; net average charge must keep rising on mix rather than on price alone; free cash flow must stop declining once franchise-acquisition spend is bridged; and the board must re-authorize a meaningful buyback in August.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that H&R Block is a bad business. It is that the business is a well-run annuity sitting directly in front of the most capable automation technology ever built, carrying a balance sheet with no shock absorber, and that one good season proves far less than the bulls think.

Start with the cash. Free cash flow fell 8.9% year over year and has compounded at negative 7.1% over three years - while earnings per share compounded at positive 10.9%. That gap is the whole game. Earnings-per-share growth here is substantially manufactured by retiring shares, not by the underlying cash engine expanding. Part of the decline is franchise buybacks, which are a legitimate investment. But management has never bridged it, no analyst has ever asked about it across five consecutive calls, and a company that is buying back stock with a shrinking cash line is drawing down a finite resource. Strip out the buyback and the growth story is a 2.8% three-year revenue compound rate - below the bottom of the 3% to 6% long-term algorithm management keeps reaffirming.

The balance sheet removes the margin for error. Tangible asset value is negative $1.12B. Working capital is negative. Net debt is $1.14B including capitalized leases ($813M excluding them). Altman-Z, a standard solvency score, sits at 2.9, in the grey zone. The much-touted return on equity of 696.8% is not a quality signal at all - it is arithmetic from a book-equity base that buybacks have driven through zero. This structure is optimized for a stable annuity. If the annuity proves unstable, the equity is levered to the downside in a way the 6.1x multiple actively disguises.

On the secular threat, the bull rebuttal proves less than claimed. One season is one data point, and the frog-boiling version of this thesis looks exactly like 2026 in year one: do-it-yourself quietly commoditized first (already visible - online paid volume was essentially flat in the 2025 season, and management chose to walk away from free filers rather than compete), then AI-equipped independents undercut the assisted channel, then the complex, high-income cohort that management has staked the entire strategy on discovers that an AI can handle a complicated return. That sequence takes five years. Campbell's 55% constant is a historical analogy, not a forecast - paper, desktop, and mobile all changed the interface to the calculation, while a large language model can replace the preparer. Management has never once quantified the downside: not a sensitivity, not a scenario, not a number, across five calls. When Sami Nasir asked directly in February 2026 whether the company's own AI tools would cannibalize its assisted business, the entire answer was that they do not think so. A qualitative history lesson is being offered in place of a quantitative risk disclosure, and thin coverage means nobody forces the issue.

The insider record is the loudest signal in the file and it points down. Zero open-market purchases against 13 sells totalling 675,730 shares. Not one officer or director has bought a single share with their own money - during a stretch when the board called the price a dislocation and spent shareholder money on it. When management's core argument is that the market misunderstands the terminal value, the cheapest possible way to prove it is a personal purchase. None has been made.

Capital allocation has also been badly timed on price. The company spent $400M buying stock at an average of $50.90 in the September 2025 quarter. It trades at $41.85 today - roughly $70M transferred to selling shareholders. And the celebrated share stabilization is a floor, not growth: Mason stated plainly in February 2026 that holding share is the high end of the guidance range. Management hit the top of its own range. That is good execution; it is not an inflection to growth, and the stock has already paid for it - up roughly 49% off the $28.16 low and 26% on the May print alone.

What would confirm the bear case: assisted share resuming its decline in the 2027 season, especially in the over-$100,000 income cohort; net average charge growth decelerating toward pure price with mix flattening; free cash flow declining again in fiscal 2027 after franchise spend is accounted for; a weak or absent buyback re-authorization in August signalling the cash is needed elsewhere; or continued insider selling into any strength.
consensus_delta:
The street is not looking the wrong way so much as it has stopped looking at all - and that is the more exploitable condition.

The hard evidence: zero price targets have been published on H&R Block in the last month and zero in the last quarter. The newest is 160 days old. At $41.85 the stock carries a 13.6% earnings yield and a 14.3% free-cash-flow yield at 6.1x enterprise value to EBITDA. That is distressed pricing. The financials are not distressed: revenue +5.3% in the latest quarter, earnings per share +23% year over year, trailing earnings per share of $5.60, gross margin stable at 44.5%, returns on invested capital of 25-39% and steady, net income at a five-year high, and a raised outlook. The precise assumption that is factually wrong: that the 2026 tax season would show AI taking share. It did not. The assisted channel HELD share, and held it favorably in every single week. Volume rose 2.1%. Refunds rose 11%. The bear case had one testable prediction and it failed its first test. Consensus has not marked this to market because there is nobody left publishing.

Where we are careful not to overclaim - and this is what keeps this from being an aggressive entry: the market is not wrong that AI is a genuine structural threat, only that it is an imminent one. One season refutes the cliff, not the slope. And the market has already partly figured this out: the stock is up roughly 49% off its February low and 26% on the May print alone. This is a re-rate in progress, not one waiting to start.
